desc:
The array nums may contain repeated values. List all distinct orderings of its elements (as sequences, each listed once) in increasing lexicographic order: compare the first elements, then the second elements, and so on. Return the k-th ordering of the list, counting from 1.

It is guaranteed that the list has at least k orderings. The list can be astronomically long, so do not generate it.

nums = [1,1,2],   k = 2  ->  [1,2,1]    (list: 112, 121, 211)
nums = [1,2,1,2], k = 4  ->  [2,1,1,2]    (list: 1122, 1212, 1221, 2112, 2121, 2211)
nums = [5],       k = 1  ->  [5]
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ 2<sup>31</sup> - 1, and k does not exceed the number of distinct orderings
hints: For a single slot, the orderings are grouped by their first value: all orderings starting with the smallest distinct value come first, then those starting with the next value, and so on.

If you fix the first value v, how many distinct orderings of the rest exist? It is a multinomial coefficient: (remaining count)! divided by the product of the factorials of the remaining multiplicities.

Walk through the distinct values in increasing order. If k is not larger than the group size, choose that value and go to the next slot. Otherwise subtract the group size from k and try the next value.
editorial: Let cnt[v] be the number of unused copies of each value and m the number of unused elements. The number of distinct orderings of those elements is m! / prod(cnt[v]!). At the current slot try the distinct values in increasing order: temporarily take one copy of v, and count the orderings of what is left, w. If k <= w the answer begins with v: keep the choice and move on. Otherwise k -= w and put the copy back.

This is the factorial number system of the plain k-th permutation problem, adapted to repeated values by using multinomial coefficients as block sizes. There are n slots, at most n distinct values each, and each count costs O(d) big-integer operations, so the time is O(n · d<sup>2</sup>) operations on numbers of at most about 150 digits (n! for n = 40); fine in Python. In languages with 64-bit integers, cap each count at 2<sup>31</sup> to avoid overflow, which is safe because k never exceeds that.
